issues.legal_issue: An agreement permitting occupation of a cooperative housing flat creates a licence rather than a lease when its terms and the circumstances show a permitted licence and no device to conceal a tenancy.
material_facts: A cooperative housing society member gave another person permission to use a flat under a written leave-and-licence agreement for successive limited terms.
The parties jointly sought and obtained the society's permission for the occupant to occupy the flat as a nominal member.
The agreement was terminated by notice, and the cooperative court found that the occupant's possession thereafter was wrongful.
The courts below found, on the evidence, that the agreement reflected a licence and not a lease.
issues.conclusion: The transaction was a licence, not a lease, and the occupant could not treat the agreement as a device concealing a tenancy.
issues.legal_principle: The parties are bound by the terms of their written leave-and-licence agreement, and the transaction is not treated as a disguised tenancy absent evidence that it was a device to conceal one. A tenant co-partner member could create a licence with the society's permission, but could not create a tenancy contrary to the society's bye-laws. The Court applied O.P. Bhatnagar v. Smt. Rukibai Narsindas, [1982] 3 SCR 681; the lower appellate court had also applied the approach in Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R.N. Kapoor, [1960] 1 SCR 368.

predicates.appeal_from_cooperative_eviction_award: A party appealed an award directing an occupant to vacate premises after permission to occupy had ended.
predicates.written_leave_and_license_agreement: A member and an occupant signed an agreement expressed to permit occupation under leave-and-licence terms.
predicates.society_permitted_nominal_occupation: The cooperative housing society permitted the occupant to occupy the premises as a nominal member.
predicates.member_could_only_grant_license: The member's status and the society's governing arrangements permitted the member to grant a licence but not to create a tenancy.
predicates.evidence_of_disguised_tenancy: Evidence showed that the stated leave-and-licence agreement was a device concealing an intended tenancy.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns an eviction award and the stated licence arrangement was permitted by the society and is not shown to conceal a tenancy, the transaction is treated as a licence rather than a lease.

issues.legal_issue: A housing society whose governing records establish that it is a tenant co-partnership society has tenant co-partner members rather than tenant owner members, and an occupant inducted under a licence cannot rely on an owner's description to establish otherwise.
material_facts: The society's registration and amended bye-laws established that it was a tenant co-partnership housing society, and the provision referring to tenant owner members had been removed.
The society had adopted the rules applicable to tenant co-partnership societies, and there was no evidence that the disputed flat belonged to a tenant owner member.
The member had permitted the occupant to use the flat under a leave-and-licence agreement after the society had adopted those rules.
The lower courts found that the member was a tenant co-partner member; the occupant argued that she was a tenant owner member and that the society was of a mixed type.
issues.conclusion: The society was a tenant co-partnership society and the member was a tenant co-partner member; the occupant could not rely on her description of herself as an owner to challenge that status.
issues.legal_principle: The society's actual classification and governing bye-laws, rather than an individual's description of a flat as owned or an obsolete or mistaken bye-law reference, determine the relevant membership status. The Court relied on O.P. Bhatnagar v. Smt. Rukibai Narsindas, [1982] 3 SCR 681, and distinguished Sabharwal Brothers v. Smt. Guna Amrit Thandani, [1973] 1 SCR 53, because it proceeded on inaccurate facts, and Ramesh Himmatlal Shah v. Harsukh Jadavji Joshi, [1975] Supp. SCR 270, which concerned attachment and sale of a member's right to occupy a flat.

issues.definition: When an eviction appeal concerns a society whose operative records establish a co-partnership structure and the occupant entered under a member's licence, the member is treated as a tenant co-partner member.

issues.legal_issue: A cooperative forum may adjudicate a member's claim to recover premises from a former licensee when the dispute concerns the society's housing business and the parties do not stand in a landlord-tenant relationship.
material_facts: A housing society formed to provide accommodation to its members permitted an occupant to use a member's flat as a nominal member under a licence.
The member terminated the licence and sought eviction through a claim under the cooperative societies legislation.
The occupant resisted the claim by asserting that the arrangement was a lease and that the rent-control court had exclusive jurisdiction.
The cooperative courts found that the relationship was one of licensor and licensee and that the dispute touched the society's business.
issues.conclusion: The cooperative courts had jurisdiction under section 91(1) of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960, and section 28 of the Bombay Rent Act did not bar the proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 91(1) of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960, a dispute concerning the business of a housing society includes a claim by the society and a member to recover premises from a person permitted to occupy them as a nominal member after revocation of a licence. The provisions of the Bombay Rent Act, including section 28, govern matters involving the landlord-tenant relationship; they do not bar cooperative proceedings where the parties do not stand in that relationship. The Court applied O.P. Bhatnagar v. Smt. Rukibai Narsindas, [1982] 3 SCR 681.
